title: Your own petition
hook: putting a short personal request into your own words, the way Sikhs do inside the Ardas

segments.voice: Yesterday, why standing, and your line: stand ready. Did you get up to answer someone? Today, the week ends with the most personal part of the Ardas. Day six hundred forty-four.

Most of the Ardas is inherited. The words about the ten Gurus, the martyrs, the gurdwaras left behind, rising spirits and good for all: these come down through generations, the same in a village in Punjab and a suburb in California. But there's one part no one can write for you. The petition. The reason today. It can be said in Punjabi, in English, in a whisper, in the words of a seven-year-old asking for her cat to get better. And it's still Ardas.
screen: `MOST OF THE ARDAS IS INHERITED.` → `ONE PART NO ONE CAN WRITE FOR YOU.` → `IN ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Sikh teaching has never treated personal asking as something embarrassing. Guru Nanak says it plainly in the Japji, in the fourth pauri, on ang 2: we speak, we beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. The asking is expected. What Sikhs often add is a sense of how to ask. A petition is called a benti, a humble request. Not a demand, not a bargain, not a list of grievances. Think back over this week. Fateh: the victory belongs to God, so you don't have to pretend you control the outcome. The Ardas before a meal: begin with thanks. Before a journey: name the task honestly. In grief: ask for the strength to accept the Will, not only for the pain to stop. In joy: thanks, with nothing added. Standing: come ready to act on what you ask. Put those together and you have something like a shape for a personal petition, without anyone handing you the words. First, what you're thankful for. Then, what you're actually asking, plainly. Then, who else it's for, because the Ardas always widens. Some Sikhs also add a line of acceptance, that whatever comes is within the Will. The words themselves are yours. Nobody grades them. Ardas said in clumsy English by a teenager at 2 a.m. is still Ardas. And Sikhs often say the honest, clumsy version is closer to the point than a beautiful one that isn't meant.
screen: `WE BEG, AND THE GIVER GIVES.` · `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `THANKS, ASK, WIDEN, ACCEPT.` · `CLUMSY AND HONEST IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three lines. If you have paper or your phone's notes, use them. If not, compose in your head. Line one: something you're thankful for, today, specifically. Line two: the one thing you most want to ask for, said plainly. Line three: someone else this is for, or someone else who needs the same. Don't polish. Don't make it sound holy. Just make it true. If you pray, you can offer those lines inside your own prayer, or after a quiet Waheguru. If not, simply read them back to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Your own petition. Inside the inherited Ardas, the reason for today is said in your own words: a benti, a humble request, in any language.
Your line: your own words. Today, keep your three lines with you, and read them once more before you sleep. Day six hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs place their own request into the Ardas at the petition, in Punjabi or any language; at home a person praying alone names their reason in their own words.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a humble request or supplication; in Gurbani often spelled ਬੇਨੰਤੀ.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ardas is a fixed prayer you recite.
what it means: the inherited Ardas holds a place for your own words, in any language.
what a scholar hears: the fixed liturgy and the free petition sit side by side; Gurbani's word benti frames asking as humble request, and the Japji takes asking for granted.

notes: Confirm the paraphrase of Japji pauri 4 ('aakhahi mangahi dehi dehi daat kare daataar').
The 'shape' of a petition (thanks, ask, widen, accept) is the narrator's summary drawn from the week's days, not a prescribed Sikh form; the script says so and gives no prayer text.
